RATIONALE: There should be a demonstrable purpose and documented need for the proposed organizational change. 1.
Explain why the organizational change is being proposed.
The current College of Education and Professional Studies (CEPS) is composed of three units: the School of Education (SOE), The School of Professional Studies (SPC), and The Office of Strategic Initiatives (OSI).
Ultimately, the proposed change is a change in name based on the dissolution of the two schools with OSI remaining as part of the new College of Education.
This proposal aligns with the new URI strategic plan.
A strong K-12 and higher education system is essential to meeting the strategic vision to “be a leading global research university that drives positive social, economic, and environmental change by contributing and instilling new knowledge to address the world’s greatest challenges.” Excellence and equity in education are among the world's greatest challenges and opportunities.

A recent Hanover Research report (2023) benchmarked the differences between standalone Colleges of Education and Education departments within interdisciplinary colleges and found that standalone colleges have an enrollment growth rate of 3.8% while education programs in interdisciplinary colleges have a declining growth rate of -6.8%.
Further, standalone Colleges of Education are more likely to employ faculty on the tenure track, while programs in interdisciplinary colleges hire an abundance of instructors with no academic rank.
The proposed shift positions URI as the only institution in the state with a standalone College of Education.
The School of Professional Studies (SPC) has very low enrollment in the current degree granting undergraduate programs.
When SPC was created, the university shifted the model of serving adult learners in Providence to serving adult learners better in all programs at URI.
That shift has left four under-enrolled degree programs in SPC.
The CEPS Dean currently has management responsibilities for the Providence campus.
However, the College (CEPS) and campus (Shepard Building) are two separate entities.

This proposal addresses the proposed change to the college unit, not the Providence Campus.
Decisions about the Providence campus building are beyond the scope of this academic unit proposal.
On January 26, 2023, the URI Faculty Senate voted to close two of the four SPC programs (Non-Profit Administration; Professional leadership Studies).
Proposals to move the remaining two programs (BIS-General Studies; BIS-Learner Designed) to Arts and Sciences are currently moving though the faculty senate approval process.
With these closures and moves, there are no remaining academic programs in the School of Professional Studies.

International Studies is a cross-disciplinary major that requires 33-48 credits.
To become an international studies major students must first become one of the approved ISD language majors.
No student may have International Studies as a single major.
No more than 50% of international studies required credits can come from any one course code.
To graduate with an international studies major, students must remain in the ISD program, which requires students to successfully concurrently complete a major in an approved language, meet the ISD language proficiency benchmark, meet minimum GPA requirements and study abroad at an ISD approved setting for at least one semester.

International Studies has three Core areas with the following requirements: 1) In the International Relations Core, students must take PSC 116G and PSC 211 and at least one of the following: PSC 300, 312*, 320, 321, 322, 325, 350, 360, 377, 408, 415, 416, 417, 419, 421G, 422, 431, 434, 435, 482*, 492. *Topic must be approved by the ISD director 2) In the International Economics Core, students must take ECN 201, 202, 358 (online study abroad course) and at least one of the following ECN 338, 344, 363. 3) In the History, Culture, and Society Core, students must take APG 203.
In addition to the above Core options, any of the following courses may be taken as major electives that count towards the 33 credits: AAF 410; APG 200, 315, 329, 415, 465; COM 361; ECN 305, 306, 381, 390, 445, FLM 451; GWS 401, 430; HIS 311, 333, 353G, 354, 373, 374, 375, 376, 377, 379, 382, 384, 385, 388; LAN 220; RLS 221. *Topic must be approved by the ISD director Students must take at least one 400-level course from any of the Core or major elective courses.

In order to transfer from University College for Academic Success to the College of Arts and Sciences, ISD students must have completed a minimum of 30 credits with a cumulative GPA of 2.50 or higher.
Once they have met these requirements and been transferred to the College of Arts and Sciences, students will be advised by three faculty coordinators (one from political Science - who also serves as M.A .director, one from economics, and one from languages).
A total of 120 credits and a cumulative GPA of 2.5 or higher is required for graduation.
At least 42 of these credits must be in courses numbered 300 or above.
Language (B.A.) Students in the ISD program must major in an approved language from the following existing majors: French, Chinese, Spanish, German, Italian, and Global Language Area Studies.
Each of the approved languages attached to the ISD program requires 30 credit hours.
ISD students must achieve B2-level (CEFR) or Advanced-Low (ACTFL) language proficiency in their target language to graduate from the ISD program.
These are the minimum required language proficiency levels for graduate or professional work in that language.
It is recommended that students take LAN 220 during their first or second year.

Study Abroad Required Study abroad at an approved international institutional setting is a key requirement for the ISD program.
ISD students are required to study abroad for at least one semester but a full academic year abroad is recommended.
Students must meet the intermediate mid (B1.1) language proficiency level or above prior to study abroad.
Upon return from study abroad students must should meet the intermediate high (B1.2) language proficiency level or above to remain in the ISD Program.
Admission, Retention and Graduation Requirements To obtain admission into the ISD Program from high school, students should have a cumulative GPA of 3.2 or above.
For existing URI students to obtain entry into the standard ISD program, they must apply by the end of the first semester of their second year, have an overall GPA 3.0 or above and have earned a C+ or above in PSC 116G.
Students must also obtain formal consultation and approval from the section head of the target language or department chair of Languages to ensure that the student is at the appropriate proficiency benchmark in order to achieve advanced low (B2) language proficiency upon completion of the program.

Existing ISD students may apply for the accelerated B.A. and M.A. program in their second semester of their third year.
To apply, students must have an overall GPA 3.0 or above and an International Studies Major GPA 3.3 or above.
To remain in the program ISD students must maintain an overall GPA 2.5 or above.
To graduate from the ISD program, the ISD Director will confirm with the Languages Department will certify that students have met the advanced low (B2) language proficiency level or above [or Advanced-Low (ACTFL)].
A copy of the proficiency paperwork must be signed by the chair of the Department of Modern and Classical Languages or the appropriate section head designee and presented communicated to the Dean’s Office ISD Director prior to graduation.
The ISD Director will confirm with the Dean’s Office that students have met all of the program requirements prior to graduation.

Rationale for closing program: In 1993, the University of Rhode Island entered into a partnership with Rhode Island College to offer a Joint PhD program in Education.
Although the intention was for the universities to share the responsibility (budget, staffing, etc.), Rhode Island College has not, in recent years, been in a position to support half of the program responsibilities.
As such, the program has largely been supported by URI (teaching faculty, graduate assistants, travel funding, etc.).
Yet, most of the tuition revenue has flowed to Rhode Island College.
In the summer of 2022, the Deans of the URI Alan Shawn Feinstein College of Education and Professional Studies (Dennis) and RIC Feinstein College of Education and Human Development (Dingus-Eason) agreed to discontinue the current Joint Program.
Faculty and students have been notified of the decision to discontinue the joint program and a teach out plan has been developed.

Dean Dennis has also been working with URI OGC to ensure that the process aligns with the agreements between URI and RIC.
The agreement between URI and RIC states that “The continuation of this program depends on the continued agreement, support, and participation of both institutions.
Termination or withdrawal of support of the program at either institution will result in termination of the program” (p. 86).
As such, the faculty in the school of education have re-designed a stand-alone Ph.D. program in Education at the University of Rhode Island.
The program proposal for that “new” program is being submitted concurrently with this closure paperwork. (See Kuali) URI Faculty have used the “best of” current courses to design a scholarly doctoral program that is more research intensive than the current joint program–which was initially designed to prepare educational practitioners.
The proposed new URI program builds on current strengths (courses, faculty, ongoing research) to produce educational scholars who can solve the most intractable contemporary education problems.

The new program will allow students to develop focused expertise in an area of PreK-20 or adult education settings that aligns with current graduate program offerings and faculty expertise in the School of Education. 13.
